newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila says to help cash-strapped rice centre.
newsitem.headline: Manila says to help cash-strapped rice centre.

text.p: The Philippines is looking at proposals for financial aid for the cash-strapped International Rice Research Institute (IRRI), Agriculture Secretary Salvador Escudero said on Wednesday.
The proposals include the extension of current funding and sourcing cash from donors, including the Philippines.
President Fidel Ramos really wants to help to make sure IRRI's strength on rice is maintained," Escudero told a news conference.
IRRI, the world's premier rice research and training centre, announced on Tuesday it was laying off half its core employees due to severe funding cuts.

"The shortfalls -- $2 million in 1996, and more than $6 million in 1997 -- stem from the inability of several of IRRI's major donors to maintain previous funding levels," the institute said in a statement.
IRRI director George Rothschild said in a previous interview the institute needs an operating budget of $31 million a year.

Escudero said he and Science and Technology Secretary William Padolina, who both sit in the IRRI board, were instructed by Ramos to find out how the government could help solve IRRI's funding shortfall.
He said members of the cabinet have proposed "sourcing" the $6 million funding requirements of IRRI. "There was one suggestion to ask funds from donors after the Philippines leads the way," he said.
IRRI was formed in 1960 by the Ford and Rockefeller Foundation to promote research in rice.

The non-profit international rice research and training centre is supported by the Consultative Group on International Agricultural Research, an association of public and private donor agencies that fund 16 international agricultural research centres worldwide.
IRRI has been credited with helping eradicate hunger by creating several high-yielding rice varieties.
IRRI scientists are now perfecting a thick-stalked rice variety that can increase present yields by up to 25 percent, or to 12 to 13 tonnes per hectare.

IRRI hopes to perfect the new strain by the turn of the century but scientists working on the new rice plant earlier told Reuters they fear that cuts in the agency's budget might hold up the research. --Manila newsroom (632) 841-89-36, Fax 817-62-67
